First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $4\pi $ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi -2\pi  & =2\pi  \\ 2\pi -2\pi  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sec}⁡0=\operatorname{sec}⁡4\pi .$

The angle $0$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14253609/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡0=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sec}⁡0=1.$
